summary: A picosecond laser used for pigmentation, dull skin tone and tattoo removal, suited to a range of Asian skin tones.
leadAnswer: Pico laser is a category of laser, not a single machine. Every pico device fires pulses lasting trillionths of a second, but they differ in wavelength, which decides which pigment, ink colours and skin tones a device suits. Kaiteki runs more than one pico platform for that reason, and a doctor decides which, if any, fits your skin.

facts.label: Matched to your skin type and pigment
Typical facial pigment appointment, including preparation
Your first visit is a doctor consultation, not a treatment

routes.title: Surface pigment
routes.body: Sun spots, freckles and other benign pigmented marks sitting in the upper skin. These are generally the most predictable pigment to treat and usually need the fewest sessions.

routes.title: Deeper and hormonal pigment
routes.body: Melasma, and dermal pigment conditions such as naevus of Ota or Hori's naevus. These sit deeper, respond less predictably, and melasma in particular is a long-term condition managed rather than finished.

routes.title: Post-acne marks and tone
routes.body: Brown marks left behind after spots have settled, along with dull or uneven overall tone and the look of enlarged pores. Active acne is managed medically first; see below.

routes.title: Tattoo ink
routes.body: Black and dark blue inks respond most predictably. Light colours, white and some cosmetic or permanent-makeup pigments can be resistant or behave unpredictably, so tattoos are assessed individually.

routesNote: Pico laser treats the marks acne leaves, not acne itself. Active inflammatory spots are usually managed medically first, with pigment work once the skin has settled.

variantModule.heading: Which pico device, and why it matters
variantModule.intro: Both platforms fire picosecond pulses, but their primary wavelengths differ, and wavelength changes how strongly melanin absorbs the pulse. That is a difference in energy delivery, not a ranking.

items.title: PicoSure
items.body: An alexandrite-wavelength platform. 755nm is absorbed strongly by melanin, which is useful for certain pigment and ink colours but makes skin tone a larger factor in the settings chosen. The manufacturer limits some indications by Fitzpatrick skin type.

items.title: Fotona PQX (StarWalker)
items.body: Built around the longer 1064nm Nd:YAG wavelength, which interacts less with surface melanin and travels deeper. Often chosen where skin tone or pigment depth makes a 755nm pass less appropriate.

variantModule.note: A single-device clinic can offer only that device's wavelength. Running two lets the device be matched to your skin, not the other way round.

ctaMid.heading: Not sure which applies to you?
ctaMid.body: A doctor can look at your skin, tell you which type of pigment you have, and say honestly whether a pico laser is the right tool for it.

avoidIf.body: This raises the risk of an uneven response and of pigment change afterwards.

avoidIf.lead: Active infection, inflammation or open skin
avoidIf.body: in the area to be treated.

avoidIf.lead: A history of keloid or hypertrophic scarring.
Recent lasers, peels or other procedures

bringToConsult: Bring your medical, medication and skincare history, including previous lasers or peels and any tendency to darken after a spot or scratch. That last detail changes the settings chosen.

sessionSteps.title: Consultation and skin assessment
sessionSteps.body: Your first visit is a doctor consultation, not a treatment. The doctor examines the area, takes your history, and explains whether a pico laser is appropriate. Sometimes the answer is a different treatment, or waiting.

sessionSteps.title: Test area where appropriate
sessionSteps.body: A small patch may be treated first, particularly for deeper pigment or for tattoo ink of unknown composition, and reviewed before a full session is booked.

sessionSteps.title: Preparation
sessionSteps.body: The skin is cleansed and eye shields are fitted. Topical numbing may be applied where the plan calls for it, most often for sensitive areas and tattoo work.

sessionSteps.title: The treatment pass
sessionSteps.body: The handpiece is passed over the area in overlapping passes. Most people describe brief snapping or hot-pinprick sensations rather than sustained pain. Treated pigment may look temporarily darker or greyish straight away, which is expected.

sessionSteps.title: Afterwards
sessionSteps.body: A cooling or soothing step, sunscreen, and aftercare instructions for the area treated. Tattoo appointments vary with size.

afterSession.intro: Downtime is usually short, but short is not none, and what you see in the first fortnight is part of the process rather than a problem.

bands.title: The first few hours
bands.body: Mild redness, warmth and sometimes slight swelling. Most people go back to their day.

bands.title: Day one to two
bands.body: Redness typically settles. Where pigment was targeted directly, treated spots often look darker than before. This is expected and not a sign the treatment has gone wrong.

bands.title: Day three to roughly two weeks
bands.body: Small darkened flecks or fine crusting may appear and then flake away on their own. Leave them alone; picking is the most common cause of a mark that outlasts the treatment.

bands.title: Between sessions
bands.body: Sessions are spaced a few weeks apart to let the skin clear treated pigment before the next pass.

afterSession.aftercare: Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen and real sun avoidance, since sun exposure between sessions is a main reason pigment returns; gentle cleansing and moisturising; and no retinoids or acids until your doctor says to resume.

risks.intro: Each is explained at consultation, before anything is booked.
risks.common: Redness, warmth, mild swelling, pinpoint bruising and small crusts that flake away over one to two weeks.
risks.lessCommon: Darkening of the treated skin after treatment (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation), lightening of the treated skin, blistering and, rarely, scarring.
risks.pigmentNote: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is the risk that matters most in the skin tones common here: skin with more melanin answers injury with more pigment, so an over-aggressive setting can leave a darker mark than the one it targeted. That is why a doctor may choose lower energy, longer intervals, a test patch or a different wavelength. A slower plan is often the safer one.
cannotDo: It does not stop new pigment forming. Without daily sun protection, sun-related marks return, and melasma in particular fluctuates with sun exposure and hormones, so it is managed long-term rather than finished in a fixed course.
It does not treat active acne. Marks left behind, yes; the inflammatory condition itself is managed medically.
It cannot promise complete clearance of a tattoo. Ink composition is rarely known with certainty, and some colours respond poorly.
It does not lift or tighten skin.
risks.disclose: Tell your doctor about anything listed under who should postpone it, and any history of cold sores.

costFactors.intro: Kaiteki does not quote prices online; the figure you get at consultation reflects your assessed plan. What moves it:
factors: Type and depth of pigment. Surface sun spots generally need fewer visits than deeper dermal pigment.
Size of the area treated, whether a few spots, a full face, or a body area.
Which device and settings your doctor selects for your skin type.
For tattoos: ink colours, density, how many layers were applied, the age of the tattoo and where it sits on the body.
How your skin responds between sessions, which is reviewed each visit.
Whether pico work is combined with other steps in a wider plan.
costFactors.outro: Facial pigment is commonly planned as several sessions a few weeks apart, reviewed as it goes; melasma is managed on an ongoing basis.

relatedReasons.microneedling: Considered where the concern is depressed acne scarring or texture rather than pigment.
relatedReasons.vascular-pigment-laser: Used where redness and visible vessels sit alongside the pigment, which a pico laser does not address.
relatedReasons.resurfacing-laser: A fractional CO2 approach, considered for deeper scarring and significant texture change.

seoTitle: Pico Laser Treatment Malaysia | Pigmentation | Kaiteki
seoDescription: Pico laser at Kaiteki uses picosecond pulses for pigmentation, uneven tone and tattoo ink. A doctor assesses which device and settings suit your skin.

sections.heading: What is Pico laser?
body: “Pico” refers to the length of the laser pulse, not to a brand. A picosecond is a trillionth of a second, and pulses that short deliver their energy faster than the surrounding skin can heat up. The effect on pigment is therefore largely photomechanical (a rapid shockwave that fractures pigment clusters) rather than thermal.

That matters because heat tends to provoke pigment problems in the skin tones common in Malaysia, which is why picosecond devices are widely used here for pigment work. Suitability still turns on three things a doctor checks: the type and depth of your pigment, your skin type, and whether you mark after inflammation.

sections.heading: How does a picosecond pulse break up pigment?
body: The pulse is absorbed by pigment far more strongly than by the surrounding skin. Because it arrives and ends in trillionths of a second, the pigment particle takes the energy as a mechanical shock and breaks into smaller fragments. Those fragments are then cleared gradually by the body's own immune cells over the weeks that follow, which is why the visible change after a pico session develops over time rather than appearing on the day.

Delivered at lower energy with a diffractive lens, the same pulse creates small zones of controlled injury in the upper skin without breaking the surface, which is used as a skin-renewal pass for texture and tone rather than for a specific mark. Wavelength, energy, spot size and lens are set per patient, not fixed.

faqs.q: What is the difference between PicoSure and Fotona PQX?
faqs.a: Both are picosecond lasers with different primary wavelengths. PicoSure's 755nm is absorbed strongly by melanin, which is useful for certain pigment and ink colours but makes skin tone a bigger factor in the settings. Fotona PQX's 1064nm interacts less with surface melanin and travels deeper. A plan may use one, the other, or both.

Most people describe brief snapping or hot-pinprick sensations rather than sustained pain, and picosecond pulses are generally reported as more tolerable than older longer-pulse lasers. Numbing cream can be used for sensitive areas and tattoo work, and settings can be adjusted during the session.

faqs.q: How many sessions will I need?
faqs.a: It depends on pigment type and depth, area size, and how your skin responds between visits. Surface sun spots generally need fewer sessions than dermal pigment or a dense tattoo. Facial pigment is commonly planned as several sessions a few weeks apart; melasma is managed on an ongoing basis.

faqs.q: What happens in the days after a session?
faqs.a: Mild redness and warmth for a few hours, sometimes slight swelling. Treated spots often look darker for a day or two, then small flecks or fine crusting flake away on their own over one to two weeks. Don't pick, keep skincare gentle, and use sunscreen daily.

faqs.q: Will I see a difference after one session?
faqs.a: Not reliably. Your body clears fragmented pigment gradually, so change develops over the weeks after each session, and deeper pigment typically needs more sessions than surface marks. Progress is reviewed at each visit.

faqs.q: Is Pico laser suitable for darker Malaysian skin tones?
faqs.a: Picosecond lasers are used across a wide range of skin tones, but skin with more melanin is more likely to darken after treatment, so settings, wavelength and intervals are chosen more conservatively and a test patch is often used. 755nm interacts more with melanin than 1064nm, which is one reason Kaiteki runs both.

Sometimes, with caution. Melasma is chronic, driven by sun and hormones, and can recur, and over-aggressive treatment can worsen it. It is usually managed as an ongoing plan of sun protection, topical care and conservative in-clinic settings, and a doctor decides whether any laser suits your melasma at all.

faqs.q: Can a tattoo be completely removed?
faqs.a: That cannot be predicted before assessment. Black and dark blue inks respond most predictably; light colours, white and some cosmetic pigments can resist or behave unpredictably. Because ink composition is rarely known, a small test area may be treated first. Size, depth, age and location affect the number of sessions.

faqs.q: How much does Pico laser cost in Malaysia?
faqs.a: Kaiteki does not quote prices online. Cost depends on pigment type and depth, area size, device and settings, number of sessions and any combined treatment, and for tattoos on ink colours and density too. Pricing is given at consultation for your assessed plan.

faqs.q: Can I wear makeup or go back to work afterwards?
faqs.a: Most people return to their day straight after a facial pigment session, and redness usually settles within hours to a day or two. Makeup can go back on once redness settles, over intact skin only and never over crusting. Daily sunscreen matters more than makeup timing.
